full_text_en:
Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources v. Nantai Real Estate Co., Ltd. — dispute over state-owned land use rights transfer contract

【Ruling Summary】

(1) According to Article 45 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, conditions attached by the parties to the validity of a contract refer to specific conditions specially agreed upon in the contract, the fulfillment or non-fulfillment of which serves as the basis for the contract to take effect or not. Such conditions must be future, uncertain, agreed-upon, and lawful facts. The authority and responsibility of a government agency to examine or approve relevant matters or contracts derive from the provisions of laws and administrative regulations and do not fall within the scope agreed upon by the parties. If the parties stipulate such authority and responsibility as a condition for the contract, it does not comply with the law.

(2) According to Article 52(5) of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 4 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China (I), the determination of a contract's invalidity shall be based on laws and administrative regulations, and shall not be based on local regulations or administrative rules. Where the land use purpose stipulated in the "State-Owned Land Use Rights Transfer Contract" signed by both parties differs from that in the planning and appraisal reports, if this may result in the land use rights transfer fee being lower than the minimum price determined by the local government in accordance with national regulations at the time of contract signing, it constitutes a factor affecting the validity of the price clause of the state-owned land use rights transfer contract, but does not render the contract void.

(3) According to Article 6 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, when engaging in civil activities, civil subjects must not only comply with laws but also, in the absence of legal provisions, comply with national policies. Notices issued by the State Council regarding the regulation and rectification of the land transfer market order, as well as supporting implementation rules issued by relevant ministries and commissions under the State Council, are national policies. According to relevant national policies, if commercial land was agreed to be transferred by agreement after July 1, 2002, without prior approval by the city or county government or the signing of a written project development agreement, it should be changed to be transferred by means of bidding, auction, or listing in accordance with relevant provisions. Perfecting the procedures for bidding, auction, or listing constitutes a modification or rescission of the relevant state-owned land use rights transfer contract, which affects whether the relevant contract can actually be performed and whether it should be rescinded, but does not affect or restrict the validity of the contract.

(4) The right of rescission is a right of formation in substantive terms and manifests as an action for formation in procedural terms. In the absence of a party filing such a claim in accordance with the law, the people's court may not directly render a judgment on its own authority.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2004) Min Yi Zhong Zi No. 106

Appellant (Defendant at First Instance): Qingdao Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources, domiciled at: Laoshan District Government Administrative Building, Qingdao, Shandong Province.

Legal Representative: Feng Yiguang, Director.

Agent ad litem: Luo Jie, Attorney at Beijing Zhongjing Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Meng Fansheng, Attorney at Beijing Zhongjing Law Firm.

Appellee (Plaintiff at First Instance): Qingdao Nantai Real Estate Co., Ltd., domiciled at: No. 2, Taipingjiao Sixth Road, Shinan District, Qingdao, Shandong Province.

Legal Representative: Song Lei, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Tang Jian, Attorney at Shandong Wanrun Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Ma Guiqin, Attorney at Shandong Wanrun Law Firm.

In the case concerning the dispute over the state-owned land use rights transfer contract between the appellant, Qingdao Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources (hereinafter referred to as the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources), and the appellee, Qingdao Nantai Real Estate Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Nantai Company), the Shandong High People's Court rendered the civil judgment (2004) Lu Min Yi Chu Zi No. 9 on September 14, 2004. The Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources, dissatisfied with the judgment of first instance, appealed to this Court. After accepting the case, this Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law and held a hearing on December 2, 2004. The agents ad litem of the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources, Luo Jie and Meng Fansheng, and the agents ad litem of Nantai Company, Tang Jian and Ma Guiqin, appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. The case is now concluded.

The court of first instance found through trial: On February 23, 2001, the Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province held an investment promotion event called "Qingdao Day" in Australia. During this event, Duanjiabu Village, Shazikou Subdistrict Office, Laoshan District, Qingdao, Shandong Province, signed the "Joint Construction Contract for the Development of the 'Australia Tourism and Holiday Village'" with Australia Nantai Real Estate Co., Ltd. and Qingdao Xincheng Real Estate Co., Ltd. Zhang Yunping, Deputy Director of the Qingdao High-tech Park Management Committee, as the authorized representative of Duanjiabu Village, Shazikou Subdistrict Office, Laoshan District, Qingdao, Shandong Province, and the Chief Executive Officer of Australia Nantai Resources Development Group as the authorized representative of Australia Nantai Real Estate Co., Ltd. and Qingdao Xincheng Real Estate Co., Ltd., and Zhou Jiabin, Deputy Mayor of the Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province, as the witness representative of Duanjiabu Village, Shazikou Subdistrict Office, Laoshan District, Qingdao, Shandong Province, and Park Keaton, Councillor of the local city hall in Australia, as the witness representative of Australia Nantai Real Estate Co., Ltd. and Qingdao Xincheng Real Estate Co., Ltd., signed the contract respectively.

On August 15, 2001, the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources, Nantai Company, and Australia Nantai Real Estate Co., Ltd. signed the "Reservation Agreement for State-Owned Land Use Rights in Laoshan District, Qingdao" (Qing Lao Tu Yu Zi (2001) No. 18). The agreement stipulated: the land is located in Duanjiabu Village, Shazikou Subdistrict Office, Laoshan District, Qingdao, Shandong Province, with a land area of 200,000 square meters, a land use rights transfer fee of RMB 210,000 per mu, totaling RMB 63 million, the planned land use is comprehensive land, with a use period of 50 years; Nantai Company and Australia Nantai Real Estate Co., Ltd. shall, based on this agreement, go through the procedures for establishing the enterprise, etc., and within the validity period of the reservation, formally sign the "State-Owned Land Use Rights Transfer Contract" with the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources to obtain the land use rights.

On October 11, 2001, the Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province approved the establishment of Nantai Company with the "Approval Certificate for Foreign-Invested Enterprises" (Shang Wai Zi Qing Fu Zi (2001) No. 0820). The approval certificate stated that the enterprise type was a Sino-foreign joint venture, with an operating period of 10 years and a registered capital of RMB 20 million, of which Australia Nantai Real Estate Co., Ltd. contributed RMB 6 million, accounting for 30% of the registered capital; Qingdao Xincheng Real Estate Co., Ltd. contributed RMB 2 million, accounting for 10%; Qingdao Furi Automobile Sales Co., Ltd. contributed RMB 6 million, accounting for 30%; and Qingdao High-tech Industrial Park Jingjia Commerce and Trade Co., Ltd. contributed RMB 6 million, accounting for 30%. The business scope included engaging in real estate development and housing sales, etc., within the 300 mu land area determined by Qing Lao Tu Yu Zi (2001) No. 18 in Duanjiabu Village, Shazikou Subdistrict Office, Laoshan District, Qingdao, Shandong Province. On November 13, 2001, the Qingdao Administration for Industry and Commerce of Shandong Province issued the "Business License for Enterprise Legal Person" to Nantai Company.

On January 24, 2002, the Laoshan District Development and Planning Bureau of Qingdao, Shandong Province, based on Nantai Company's application, issued the "Reply on the Approval of the 'Australia Garden' Project Proposal" (Lao Ji Xiang Zi (2002) No. 29), approving the implementation of the Australia Garden development project. The reply stated: 1. Project content: Construction of the Australia Garden residential community, including residences, apartments, and villas. 2. The project is located in Duanjiabu Village, Shazikou Subdistrict Office, with a total land area of 200,000 square meters and a total construction area of 260,000 square meters. 3. The planned total investment for the project is RMB 350 million, with funds to be raised by Nantai Company itself. 4. The project is scheduled to start in October 2002, with a construction period of 3 years. 5. The project may only commence construction after completing the approval procedures for land use, planning, environmental protection, fire protection, etc.

On February 4, 2002, the Qingdao Planning Bureau of Shandong Province issued the "Review Opinion on Construction Project Planning" (Qing Gui Han Zi (2002) No. 84). The opinion stated that, based on the Urban Planning Law of the People's Republic of China and relevant regulations and urban planning requirements, the reply opinion was as follows: (1) According to the overall planning of Shazikou Town approved by the Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province, the planned land use nature for the project land is residential land. The development nature is consistent with the planned land use nature, and the site selection and construction are approved. (2) Considering the current construction and planning status around the proposed land, to coordinate the development and construction of the surrounding area and comprehensive supporting facilities for various types, the construction unit is required to, based on the overall planning of Shazikou and in accordance with the requirements of the "Urban Planning Compilation Measures", first prepare a control detailed planning plan for the area enclosed by the red line shown on the west side of the Han River in the diagram. (3) It is requested to go to the Laoshan Branch of the Qingdao Planning Bureau of Shandong Province to confirm the blue line of the river and the red and green lines of the surrounding and internal roads. (4) The control detailed planning for the above area should be prepared promptly and submitted to the Qingdao Planning Bureau of Shandong Province for approval before proceeding with relevant planning procedures.

On July 29, 2002, the Qingdao Planning Bureau of Shandong Province issued the "Notice on Conditions for Construction Land Planning and Design", agreeing that Nantai Company could carry out planning and design of the land according to the planning and design conditions.

On December 26, 2002, the Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province submitted to the Shandong Provincial People's Government the "Request for Instructions on the 18th Batch of Urban Construction Land in Laoshan District in 2002". The request stated that, upon review, the land in that batch was consistent with the overall land use plan of Shazikou Subdistrict Office, Laoshan District. Within the determined construction land area, the occupied farmland had been developed and supplemented with an equal amount of farmland and had passed acceptance, and it was proposed to approve the land as the 18th batch of urban construction land in Laoshan District in 2002 and to go through the procedures for conversion of agricultural land and land acquisition. After the land was approved, the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources would manage it as reserve land. When specific projects were arranged, land would be supplied separately in accordance with national regulations. The paid land use fee was to be borne by the Laoshan District People's Government.

On December 27, 2002, the Laoshan Branch of the Qingdao Planning Bureau of Shandong Province issued the "Review Opinion on Construction Project Planning Scheme", agreeing in principle to the road engineering planning and design schemes for lines 8, 10, 12, 15, 17, and 19 in Shazikou submitted by Nantai Company, and requiring Nantai Company to submit the construction drawings for review.

On January 6, 2003, the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources and Nantai Company signed the "State-Owned Land Use Rights Transfer Contract". Article 3 of the contract stipulated: The parcel of land transferred by the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources to Nantai Company is located in Duanjiabu Village, Shazikou Subdistrict Office, with a parcel area of 186,235 square meters, of which the transferred land area is 152,702 square meters. Article 4 stipulated: The purpose of the transferred land is residential. Article 6 stipulated: The transfer term is 50 years. Article 7 stipulated: The transfer fee is RMB 369.15 per square meter, with a total amount of RMB 56,369,943.3. Article 15 stipulated: Within 30 days from the date Nantai Company pays the full land use rights transfer fee in accordance with this contract, it shall hold this contract and the payment voucher for the land use rights transfer fee, and apply to the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources for land registration in accordance with regulations, to obtain the "State-Owned Land Use Rights Certificate" and the transferred land use rights. The Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources shall, within 30 days from the date of accepting the land registration application, handle the transferred land use rights registration for Nantai Company in accordance with the law and issue the "State-Owned Land Use Rights Certificate". Article 40(2) stipulated: The land transfer plan under this contract is subject to the approval of the Shandong Provincial People's Government, and this contract shall take effect from the date of approval by the Shandong Provincial People's Government. Article 45 stipulated: Matters not covered in this contract shall be agreed upon by both parties as appendices to the contract, which shall have the same legal effect as the contract. On the same day, the two parties reached a "Supplementary Agreement" on matters not covered in this contract. Article 4 of the "Supplementary Agreement" stipulated: According to Article 3 of the contract, the total parcel area is 186,235 square meters, of which the net land area is 152,702 square meters. Nantai Company agrees to expropriate roads and green belts with an area of 33,533 square meters on its behalf, at a price of RMB 50,000 per mu, totaling RMB 2,514,975, and shall bear the relevant taxes and fees and compensation for ground attachments. After the final land area is determined, the land area in this clause shall be adjusted accordingly. Article 5 stipulated: The time for the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources to supply the land shall commence from the date this contract is approved. Article 6 stipulated: This agreement shall take effect upon being signed and sealed by both the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources and Nantai Company.

On January 13, 2003, the Qingdao Planning Bureau of Shandong Province issued to Nantai Company the "Construction Land Planning Permit" (Qing Gui Yong Di Zi (2003) No. 3), stating that the "Australia Garden" project land complied with urban planning requirements and that planning and land use procedures were allowed to proceed.

On February 19, 2003, the Shandong Provincial People's Government issued the "Reply on the 18th Batch of Urban Construction Land in Laoshan District, Qingdao in 2002" (Lu Zheng Tu Zi (2003) No. 52), agreeing that Qingdao should convert 200,000 square meters of agricultural land in Shazikou Subdistrict Office, Laoshan District, into construction land, including 66,191 square meters of farmland and 133,809 square meters of garden land. After the conversion of the above agricultural land, it was approved for expropriation for urban construction in Qingdao, Shandong Province.

On April 12, 2004, the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources, on the grounds that the "State-Owned Land Use Rights Transfer Contract" was invalid and that it could not fulfill the obligations agreed upon in the contract, notified Nantai Company to rescind the "State-Owned Land Use Rights Transfer Contract" signed by both parties and requested Nantai Company to go to the Laoshan District Commercial Land Contract Clearing Office within 30 days after receiving the notice to handle refund and other related matters. On June 18, 2004, the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources sent to Nantai Company the "Letter on Urgently Handling the Refund Procedures for Land Transfer Fees", requesting Nantai Company to go to the Laoshan District Commercial Land Contract Clearing Office within 15 days after receiving this letter to handle the refund of land transfer fees and other related procedures; otherwise, the Laoshan District Commercial Land Contract Clearing Office would refund the land transfer fees already paid by Nantai Company in accordance with legal procedures.

It was also found: From September 28, 2001, to May 29, 2003, Nantai Company paid in full the land transfer fee of RMB 56,369,943.3 as stipulated in the transfer contract and the land expropriation fee for roads and green belts of RMB 2,514,975 as stipulated in the "Supplementary Agreement", totaling RMB 58,884,918.3.

On June 28, 2004, Nantai Company filed a lawsuit with the court of first instance, alleging: Nantai Company is the developer of the "Australia Garden" project in Qingdao. The "State-Owned Land Use Rights Transfer Contract" was signed for the land of this project. This project was a project introduced by the Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province through investment promotion, and the project and the project company established for it were legally approved by the Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province. On February 19, 2003, the Shandong Provincial People's Government approved the conversion of agricultural land and land acquisition procedures for the land involved in the Australia Garden project with Lu Zheng Tu Zi (2003) No. 52. The Qingdao Planning Bureau of Shandong Province and its Laoshan Branch, the Laoshan District Development and Planning Bureau, and the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources handled various planning procedures required for the "Australia Garden" project for Nantai Company. Based on the "Reservation Agreement for State-Owned Land Use Rights" signed by Nantai Company and the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources on August 15, 2001, the two parties formally signed the "State-Owned Land Use Rights Transfer Contract" on January 6, 2003. After signing the contract, Nantai Company not only fulfilled its obligations as agreed but also paid RMB 5 million in land compensation fees to local villagers and assisted the local village committee in handling pension insurance and other related matters for all villagers. However, the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources not only failed to handle the "State-Owned Land Use Rights Certificate" for Nantai Company as agreed, but also, on the grounds that the contract was invalid, orally notified Nantai Company to rescind the contract in July 2003, sent a written notice to rescind the contract on April 12, 2004, and sent a letter on June 18 of the same year urging Nantai Company to handle the refund procedures. The actions of the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources not only constituted a serious breach of contract but also caused incalculable economic losses to Nantai Company. To protect its legitimate rights and interests, Nantai Company specially requested a judgment ordering the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources to continue performing the "State-Owned Land Use Rights Transfer Contract" and immediately issue a land use rights certificate to Nantai Company.

The Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources orally responded: The "State-Owned Land Use Rights Transfer Contract" signed by the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources and Nantai Company has not taken effect, and the contract is not binding on either party. It requested the court of first instance to issue a judgment dismissing Nantai Company's claims.

The court of first instance held, after trial, that the focus of the dispute between the parties was: whether the "State-Owned Land Use Rights Transfer Contract" took effect and whether it was valid; and whether the "State-Owned Land Use Rights Transfer Contract" should continue to be performed.

Regarding the issue of whether the "State-Owned Land Use Rights Transfer Contract" took effect and whether it was valid. According to Article 40(2) of the "State-Owned Land Use Rights Transfer Contract", the condition for the contract to take effect was that "the land transfer plan under this contract is subject to the approval of the Shandong Provincial People's Government, and this contract shall take effect from the date of approval by the Shandong Provincial People's Government." Upon investigation, the "Australia Garden" project involved in this case was a project introduced by the Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province through investment promotion activities. After the project was introduced, the relevant procedures for project approval, planning, and land use related to the project were approved by the relevant functional departments of the Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province. On December 26, 2002, the Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province submitted to the Shandong Provincial People's Government the "Request for Instructions on the 18th Batch of Urban Construction Land in Laoshan District in 2002", which included the land involved in this case. On February 19, 2003, the Shandong Provincial People's Government approved the land request of the Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province with the "Reply on the 18th Batch of Urban Construction Land in Laoshan District, Qingdao in 2002". At this point, the condition for the "State-Owned Land Use Rights Transfer Contract" signed by both parties to take effect had been fulfilled, and the contract took effect from the date of the Shandong Provincial People's Government's reply. Whether the request submitted by the Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province included the "transfer plan" as agreed in the contract did not affect the validity of the contract. The Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources' defense that the "State-Owned Land Use Rights Transfer Contract" had not taken effect was not established and was not supported. The "State-Owned Land Use Rights Transfer Contract" and the "Supplementary Agreement" signed by both parties had lawful content and represented true intentions, and were valid contracts.

Concerning the issue of whether the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract should continue to be performed. Nantai Company, in accordance with the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract and the Supplementary Agreement, paid in full the land grant fee and the expropriation fee for the road and green land to be requisitioned. The relevant functional departments of the Qingdao Municipal People's Government, Shandong Province, handled procedures for project approval, planning, and the conversion of agricultural land to construction land and expropriation for this project. The contractual obligations of both parties had been substantially fulfilled. According to Article 15 of the contract, provided that the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources continued to perform its contractual obligations and handle the State-owned Land Use Rights Certificate for Nantai Company as agreed, the purpose of the contract could be achieved. Therefore, Nantai Company's claim requesting the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources to continue performing the contract was supported. Accordingly, the judgment was: (1) The Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources and Nantai Company shall continue to perform the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract signed on January 6, 2003; (2) The Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources shall, within 30 days after the judgment takes effect, handle the State-owned Land Use Rights Certificate for Nantai Company. The case acceptance fee of RMB 291,859.72 and the property preservation fee of RMB 281,849.72 were both borne by the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources.

The Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to this court, requesting that the first-instance judgment be overturned, and that the court amend the judgment to dismiss Nantai Company's claims, and order Nantai Company to bear the litigation fees for the first instance and the appeal as well as the property preservation fees. The main facts and reasons were:

(I) The first-instance judgment's finding that the conditions for the entry into effect of the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract signed between the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources and Nantai Company had been fulfilled did not conform to the facts and the law.

1. The State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract involved in this case was a contract contingent upon a condition precedent, and the condition had not been fulfilled. The parties explicitly agreed on the condition for the contract's entry into effect. Article 40 of the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract stipulated: "The grant plan for the parcel of land under this contract is still subject to approval by the Shandong Provincial People's Government. This contract shall take effect on the date of such approval by the Shandong Provincial People's Government." Article 5 of the Supplementary Agreement signed by the parties also stipulated: The time for the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources to supply the land shall be from the date of approval of this contract. Article 45 of the Contract Law provides: "The parties may agree on conditions for the validity of a contract. A contract contingent upon a condition becomes effective when the condition is fulfilled." In this case, the condition for the contract's entry into effect agreed upon by the parties, namely, the grant plan for the parcel under this contract, had never been approved by the Shandong Provincial People's Government. According to national laws and regulations, only after the land supply plan (including the grant plan) is approved by the people's government with the authority to approve it, can the land administration department of the city or county people's government sign a State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract with the land user. Article 22 of the Implementing Regulations of the Land Administration Law of the People's Republic of China clearly stipulates: "The construction entity shall, with the relevant approval documents for the construction project, submit an application for the use of construction land to the land administration department of the city or county people's government. The land administration department of the city or county people's government shall review the application, prepare a land supply plan, and report it to the city or county people's government for approval; if approval from a higher-level people's government is required, it shall be reported to that higher-level people's government for approval. After the land supply plan is approved, the city or county people's government shall issue a construction land approval certificate to the construction entity. For the compensated use of state-owned land, the land administration department of the city or county people's government shall sign a compensated use contract for state-owned land with the land user." It can be seen that the approval of the land supply plan is a necessary step and a prerequisite for the land administration department of the city or county people's government to sign a land grant contract. In practice, there are also cases where the contract is signed first and then reported for approval. Because of this situation, the standard form contract State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract, supervised by the Ministry of Land and Resources and the State Administration for Industry and Commerce, states in point 7 of the "Instructions for Use" at the beginning: "Regarding the provisions on contract validity in Article 40 of the contract, if the parcel grant plan has been approved by the authorized people's government, the contract shall take effect according to the first paragraph; if the parcel grant plan has not been approved by the authorized people's government, the contract shall take effect according to the second paragraph." When signing the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract, the parties made the second choice regarding the provisions on contract validity in Article 40, namely, "The grant plan for the parcel of land under this contract is still subject to approval by the Shandong Provincial People's Government. This contract shall take effect on the date of such approval by the Shandong Provincial People's Government." Moreover, according to the provisions of the Measures of Shandong Province for Implementing the Land Administration Law of the People's Republic of China, the grant plan in this case should be approved by the Shandong Provincial People's Government. The practice is that the land user submits an application to the local land administration department of the city or county people's government where the construction project is located. The local land administration department of the city or county people's government prepares the grant plan and reports it to the people's government at the same level for approval; if approval from a higher-level people's government is required, it is further reported to that higher-level people's government for approval. According to Article 24 of the Measures of Shandong Province for Implementing the Land Administration Law of the People's Republic of China, formulated by the Standing Committee of the Shandong Provincial People's Congress on August 22, 1999: "The occupation of land exceeding 8 hectares shall be approved by the provincial people's government." This is a provision of Shandong Province's local regulation regarding the examination and approval authority for the use of state-owned construction land for construction projects. The area of land to be granted under the contract in this case was 15.27 hectares, which legally should be approved by the Shandong Provincial People's Government. Since the grant plan involved in this case has never been approved by the Shandong Provincial People's Government, the condition for the contract's entry into effect has never been fulfilled.

2. The first-instance judgment confused the two different types of approval — the approval of the grant plan by the government and the approval of the conversion of agricultural land to construction land — and erroneously found that the approval of the conversion of agricultural land to construction land constituted approval of the grant plan. The passage and acquisition of approval for the conversion of agricultural land to construction land is a prerequisite for formulating the land supply plan. The land supply plan includes the allocation plan and the grant plan. The reason why the land supply plan (including the grant plan) requires approval is because Article 11 of the Urban Real Estate Administration Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "The granting of land use rights shall be carried out by the city or county people's government in a planned and step-by-step manner. The plan for each parcel of land to be granted, its use, duration, and other conditions shall be jointly formulated by the land management department of the city or county people's government together with the urban planning, construction, and real estate management departments, and shall be submitted, in accordance with the regulations of the State Council, to the people's government with the authority to approve it for approval. Thereafter, the land management department of the city or county people's government shall implement it." According to Article 10, paragraph 4, of the Measures for the Examination and Approval of Construction Land Applications, the land supply plan (including the grant plan) shall include the method of land supply, area, use, standard and amount of the compensated use fee for the land, etc. It can be seen that the approval of the conversion of agricultural land to construction land is a prerequisite for the approval of the land supply plan (including the grant plan), and the two cannot be equated. The first-instance court conflated the two, and, in a situation where the parties had explicitly agreed in the contract that the approval of the grant plan would be the condition for the contract's entry into effect, erroneously found that the condition for the entry into effect of the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract signed by the parties had been fulfilled merely because the Shandong Provincial People's Government approved the request for conversion of agricultural land submitted by the Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province. The approval document issued by the Shandong Provincial People's Government in response to the Qingdao Municipal People's Government's land use request was an approval for the conversion of 200,000 square meters of agricultural land, including the parcel under the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract, to construction land; it was not an approval of the grant plan. The first-instance judgment's finding that the conditions for the entry into effect of the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract signed by the parties had been fulfilled lacks factual and legal basis.

(II) The first-instance judgment's finding that the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract signed by the parties was a valid contract cannot stand.

1. The State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract signed by the parties seriously violated Article 8 of the Urban Real Estate Administration Law, which provides that "land owned by collectives within urban planning zones may be transferred for value only after it has been lawfully expropriated and converted into state-owned land." The Shandong Provincial People's Government, in its document titled "Reply on the Approval of the 18th Batch of Urban Construction Land for 2002 in Laoshan District, Qingdao City" dated February 19, 2003, agreed that Qingdao City could convert 200,000 square meters of agricultural land in Shazikou Subdistrict Office, Laoshan District, to construction land. The said agricultural land was to be expropriated after conversion for urban construction in Qingdao City. However, the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract involved in this case was signed as early as January 6, 2003, at which time the agricultural land had not yet been expropriated and converted into state-owned land. Construction land must be expropriated first before a grant contract is signed; this is a mandatory provision of the Real Estate Administration Law. The State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract involved in this case violated this mandatory provision. Therefore, the contract has been void ab initio.

2. The State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract signed by the parties seriously violated the relevant mandatory provisions of the state concerning the granting of state-owned land use rights through tender, auction, or listing. The Provisions on the Grant of State-Owned Land Use Rights through Tender, Auction, or Listing, issued by the Ministry of Land and Resources, came into effect as early as July 1, 2002, whereas the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract involved in this case was signed on January 6, 2003. Article 4 of the Provisions on the Grant of State-Owned Land Use Rights through Tender, Auction, or Listing stipulates: "Various types of commercial land, such as for commerce, tourism, entertainment, and commercial residential housing, must be granted through tender, auction, or listing." According to this provision, the land under the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract in this case had to be granted publicly through tender, auction, or listing. Yet the parties signed the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract by agreement six months after the Provisions on the Grant of State-Owned Land Use Rights through Tender, Auction, or Listing had come into effect, granting state-owned land for residential construction. This violated the state's regulations on granting state-owned land use rights through tender, auction, or listing, and also violated the relevant provisions of the Notice on Strictly Implementing the Grant of Commercial Land Use Rights through Tender, Auction, or Listing (Guotuzifa (2002) No. 265), jointly issued by the Ministry of Land and Resources and the Ministry of Supervision. Therefore, this State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract is a null and void contract.

3. In addition to the circumstances rendering the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract invalid as mentioned above, during the process of signing the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract, Nantai Company also had the suspicion of malicious collusion with Yu Zhijun, the former director of the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources, harming the interests of the state. This can be glimpsed from the process of land valuation. Taking August 13, 2002, as the valuation date, the valuation price of the land under this case commissioned by Nantai Company from Qingdao Eastern Real Estate Valuation Consulting Co., Ltd. was RMB 369.15 per square meter. Based on this, the grant fee payable by Nantai Company was determined to be RMB 56,369,943.3. In handling the case reported by the public concerning this matter, the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources commissioned another appraisal by Qingdao Hengyuan Appraisal Co., Ltd., which resulted in a valuation price of RMB 1,001.9 per square meter. If the land grant fee were to be paid by Nantai Company based on this, it would amount to RMB 152,992,133.8. That is, the valuation price per square meter differed by nearly three times, and the difference in the land grant fee was as large as RMB 96,622,190.5. According to Article 10 of the Interim Measures for the Administration of Urban Real Estate Market Valuation, each land valuation project must be undertaken by at least two appraisers. However, the Land Valuation Report prepared by Qingdao Eastern Real Estate Valuation Consulting Co., Ltd., commissioned by Nantai Company, was made by only one appraiser. The land use at the time of valuation was comprehensive use, but in the grant contract it changed to residential use. Furthermore, the instructions for use of the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract stipulate that the land use in Article 4 of the contract should be filled in according to the secondary classification of land in the Urban Cadastral Survey Procedures. For land with comprehensive use, the specific types of use and their respective area proportions should be stated. The land use in the signed grant contract differs from both the planning and the valuation report.

(III) The first-instance judgment, by rendering a judgment in favor of Nantai Company's claims, erroneously negated the corrective actions taken by the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources, in line with the directives of the central and various levels of government, to rectify the illegal land grant. Since the reform and opening up, due to the lack of experience in land management and legislative lag on the part of the Chinese government, coupled with collusion between some real estate developers and individual officials, driven by the temptation of huge profits, some resorted to illegal means to seize land, resulting in chaos in the state's land grant order, large areas of land falling under the control of a few individuals, and serious loss of state-owned assets. Since 2001, the State Council has issued a series of policies and regulations to strictly rectify and standardize land grant practices. This case arose against the backdrop of this national effort to rectify and regulate the land management order. With the high attention of the Shandong Provincial People's Government, after thorough investigation and study of the grant conduct in this case, the Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province determined that the grant of this parcel was illegal, instructed the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources to investigate and deal with it according to law, and classified this grant conduct as one of the key cases of violation of laws and regulations.

The first-instance judgment found that as long as the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources handled the State-owned Land Use Rights Certificate for Nantai Company as agreed, the purpose of the contract could be achieved. This is erroneous. According to the provisions of China's land administration laws and regulations, only after the land grant plan has been approved by the authorized people's government does the land administration department have the authority to sign a grant contract with the counterparty based on the approved grant plan. In this case, the land administration department had not obtained approval from the authorized people's government before signing the contract, hence the agreement that the contract would only become effective upon such approval. Now that the government has determined that the grant of this parcel was illegal, the government will not approve the grant plan for this parcel, and the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources is simply unable to continue performing the contractual obligations. If, according to the content of the first-instance judgment, the State-owned Land Use Rights Certificate were to be issued to Nantai Company, it would not only negate the corrective actions taken by the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources in the process of rectifying the land market order against the illegal grant of land to Nantai Company, conflicting with the directives of the central and various levels of government, but would also be inconsistent with the provisions of relevant laws and regulations. Therefore, whether considered from the legal perspective of the contract not having taken effect or being void, or from the perspective of implementing the directives of the central and various levels of government, the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract signed by the parties is no longer capable of performance. If the appellate court does not support the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources' appeal request, the result would be that the contract cannot be performed, and the rights claimed by the party would also be unenforceable. Therefore, the appellant requests that the appellate court ascertain the facts, render a judgment realistically, and even if it determines the contract to be valid, take into account the fact that, due to legal and factual obstacles, the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources is already unable to continue performing the contract in this case, and deliver a lawful, reasonable, and fair judgment.

(IV) The first-instance judgment exceeded the scope of civil adjudication, expanded the scope of the judgment, and violated the principle of "no trial without complaint" in civil procedure law. Nantai Company's claims in its civil complaint were two: 1. An order that the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources continue to perform the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract signed by both parties; 2. An order that the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources bear the case acceptance fee, preservation fee, and other litigation costs (during the trial, Nantai Company withdrew its original claim for damages against the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources). It can be seen that Nantai Company's substantive claim was only one: "continue to perform the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract." However, in addition to supporting Nantai Company's claim, the first-instance judgment added another item: that the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources handle the State-owned Land Use Rights Certificate for Nantai Company within 30 days after the judgment takes effect. This item was not raised as a claim by Nantai Company in its complaint. The first-instance court, by rendering a judgment exceeding the parties' claims, violated the principle of "no trial without complaint" in civil procedure law. Additionally, the issuance of a State-owned Land Use Rights Certificate is, in nature, an administrative act of the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources. A first-instance court, in the trial and judgment of a civil case, has no authority to order a party to perform an administrative act. Therefore, the first-instance judgment both exceeded the scope of the parties' claims and exceeded the limits of civil adjudication, and should be reversed.

(V) The first-instance judgment also had the following problems in finding facts and applying law: 1. It confused the relationship between the Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province and the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources, treating the administrative act of the Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province as an act of the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources in performing the contract. The project in this case was not a project introduced by the Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province. The Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province was not a party to the Joint Construction Contract for the Development of the "Australian Tourism and Holiday Village", and the contract signed violated the mandatory provisions of the Land Administration Law and is a null and void contract. 2. It unreasonably adopted property preservation measures and ordered the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources to bear the property preservation fee. 3. It erroneously found that the relevant functional departments of the Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province had handled procedures such as project approval and planning for the project, and that the contractual obligations of both parties had been substantially fulfilled. 4. It did not adopt the large amount of evidence submitted by the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources in the first instance, nor did it provide reasons.

Nantai Company argued in its defense that the facts and reasons on which the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources based its appeal were untenable, and requested that the appeal be dismissed and the original judgment be affirmed. The main facts and reasons were:

(I) The first-instance judgment's finding that the conditions for the entry into effect of the State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract signed by the parties had been fulfilled conformed to the facts and the law.

1. According to the provisions of the current Land Administration Law, its Implementing Regulations, and other laws and administrative regulations, in the case of grants of state-owned land use rights, for the type of land involved in this case, only the plan for conversion of agricultural land, the plan for supplementing cultivated land, and the plan for expropriation of land need to be approved by the provincial people's government. In this case, the Shandong Provincial People's Government had already approved the above matters through Document Luzhengtuzi (2003) No. 52.

2. Precisely because only the above matters require approval by the provincial people's government by law, the condition for the contract's entry into effect set forth in Article 40 of the contract, namely "The grant plan for the parcel of land under this contract is still subject to approval by the Shandong Provincial People's Government. This contract shall take effect on the date of such approval by the Shandong Provincial People's Government," can only refer to the approval of the plan for conversion of agricultural land, the plan for supplementing cultivated land, and the plan for expropriation of land within the parcel grant plan. As for other matters, the Shandong Provincial People's Government has neither the legal authority to approve them nor such an obligation. Even if the contract used the imprecise term "parcel grant plan," its true meaning must be determined in accordance with the law, and whether the contract has taken effect should be examined based on that.

3. In its appeal, the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources confused the approval of the land supply plan, the parcel land transfer plan, the agricultural land conversion plan, the farmland reclamation plan, and the land requisition plan. Its argument that the State-owned Land Use Right Grant Contract involved in this case was not effective is untenable. (1) The approval of the land supply plan is not a condition precedent for the effectiveness of the contract as agreed by the parties. (2) The approving authority for the land supply plan is not the Shandong Provincial People's Government according to law, but the Laoshan District People's Government of Qingdao, Shandong Province. The legal basis is Article 22, paragraph (2) of the Regulations on the Implementation of the Land Administration Law of the PRC. (3) None of the legal provisions cited by the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources in its appeal stipulate that the land supply plan (or the so-called transfer plan) should be approved by the Shandong Provincial People's Government. Its citation of Article 24 of the Measures of Shandong Province for Implementing the Land Administration Law of the PRC to argue that the approving authority for the land supply plan is the Shandong Provincial People's Government is also erroneous, because, judging from the chapter where this article is located, it provides for the approval authority for the conversion of agricultural land, not the approval authority for the land supply plan. In summary, the first-instance judgment's finding that the conditions precedent for the effectiveness of the grant contract had been fulfilled is entirely consistent with the facts and the law.

(2) The first-instance judgment's finding that the State-owned Land Use Right Grant Contract signed by the parties is valid is entirely correct. The content of the grant contract signed by the parties does not violate the mandatory provisions of laws and administrative regulations. The elements of the contract, including the parties, the subject matter, and the expression of intent, are all lawful. As for the so-called illegal issues listed by the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources in its appeal, they are all caused by the Bureau's arbitrary misinterpretation of legal provisions and intentional avoidance of legal provisions, and are fundamentally untenable. (1) The Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources has a mistaken understanding of the Real Estate Administration Law. Article 8 of that Law provides: "Collectively owned land within urban planning areas may be transferred for consideration only after it has been lawfully requisitioned and converted into state-owned land." The Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources arbitrarily misinterpreted this provision as: "For collectively owned land within urban planning areas, a grant contract (paid transfer) may be signed only after the land has been lawfully requisitioned and converted into state-owned land." Hence it reached the erroneous conclusion that "construction land must be requisitioned first, and then a grant contract may be signed." The original legislative intent of this provision is to emphasize that no actual transfer or transfer result may occur unless collectively owned land has been lawfully requisitioned and converted into state-owned land. That is, this provision restricts the specific time for performance of the Land Use Right Grant Contract, not the time for signing the contract, and the law cannot impose restrictions on the time for signing a contract. Moreover, at the time the grant contract in this case was signed, it was agreed that the contract would be subject to the condition that the land requisition and other matters be approved, and that condition precedent has been fulfilled. The Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources has already signed a land requisition contract with the original land owner and has completed performance of the requisition. (2) The Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources intentionally avoided the relevant provisions of the state on the transfer of state-owned land use rights by means of tender, auction, or listing. When arguing whether the land involved in this case could be transferred by agreement, the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources intentionally avoided the State Land and Resources Document No. (365), i.e., the Ministry of Land and Resources' Opinions on Handling Certain Issues in Self-examination and Self-correction during the Further Rectification of the Land Market Order. Article 3 of that Opinion explicitly provides for the handling of matters left over from before the implementation of the Provisions on the Transfer of State-owned Land Use Rights by Tender, Auction, or Listing. According to that provision, the land involved in this case could be transferred by agreement. The Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources ignored the fact that Document No. 365 had been promulgated and implemented, and its argument that the grant contract is invalid is erroneous. (3) As for the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources' mention that Nantai Company may have maliciously colluded with Yu Zhijun, former director of the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources, during the signing of the grant contract, thereby harming state interests, this is purely a slander against Nantai Company. Regarding the appraisal issue, during the "investigation period" of more than one year before Nantai Company filed the lawsuit in the first-instance court, the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources never raised this issue with Nantai Company. The appraisal of the land in this case complied with the legal provisions in effect at the time. As to how many appraisers should sign the appraisal report, the law has no explicit provision.

(3) The so-called "rectification action" is irrelevant to this case. The content of the anonymous report—that Nantai Company was a fake foreign investor, that it invested no money, and that the land payment was overdue—are all contrary to the facts. The land in this case had already passed the review and acceptance of the five ministries and commissions of the State Council, the Provincial Department of Land and Resources, and other departments. It was the malicious anonymous report that triggered the so-called "rectification." The Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources, disregarding the fact that the content of the report was false, went straight to the topic of taking back the land. Moreover, in the process from the report to the formal notice of taking back the land, the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources repeatedly sought reasons (not the reasons in the report) for taking back the land. Only when all the reasons it sought were untenable did it ultimately give the notice of termination of the contract with the stated reasons, and those termination reasons are unrelated to the so-called report.

(4) The first-instance judgment did not exceed the scope of trial. Regarding the request for the court to order the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources to handle the issuance of the State-owned Land Use Certificate for Nantai Company, when Nantai Company read out the first request in its complaint—requesting the court to order the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources to continue performing the contract signed by the parties—it specifically clarified that the substantive content of continued performance was the handling of the State-owned Land Use Certificate for Nantai Company, and this was recorded in the court record. Therefore, the first instance did not exceed the scope of trial and did not violate the principle of "no trial without complaint." Furthermore, issuing the State-owned Land Use Certificate is an obligation of the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources under the civil contract, and this judgment content does not exceed the scope of civil trial.

(5) The first-instance judgment did not confuse the relationship between the Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province and the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources. The primary obligations of the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources under the State-owned Land Use Right Grant Contract in this case are to provide the land and to handle the land certificate for Nantai Company. The performance of these obligations involves the approval procedures that must be handled according to law. Those procedures are a necessary step for the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources to perform the above obligations and are also its duty.

(6) The litigation preservation measures were necessary and proper, and the costs thereof should be borne by the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources. In this case, while Nantai Company was actively reporting to the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources and its superiors, requesting fair and lawful handling, the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources, on April 12, 2004, notified Nantai Company in writing of the termination of the contract and, on June 18 of the same year, processed the refund procedure with a 15-day deadline, otherwise legal action would be taken. If Nantai Company had not taken preservation measures, the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources could have deposited the land payment and separately transferred the land. Therefore, Nantai Company's application for preservation was necessary and proper.

Upon further investigation by this Court in the second instance, the following was found: Qingdao Xincheng Real Estate Co., Ltd. is a shareholder of Nantai Company, holding 10% of its shares. On August 15, 2001, when the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources signed the "Reservation Agreement for State-owned Land Use Rights in Laoshan District, Qingdao" with Nantai Company and Australia Nantai Real Estate Co., Ltd., Lu Guoqiang was the general manager of Nantai Company and signed the reservation agreement as the representative of Nantai Company.

It was further found that on February 19, 2003, the Shandong Provincial People's Government issued Lu Zheng Tu Zi (2003) No. 52 "Reply on the Approval of the Eighteenth Batch of Urban Construction Land in the Year 2002 in Laoshan District, Qingdao." In addition to approving the conversion of 200,000 square meters of agricultural land in Shazikou Subdistrict Office, Laoshan District into construction land, and the requisition of the said land after conversion for urban construction in Qingdao, it also stated that land should be provided to specific construction projects strictly in accordance with relevant provisions, and that the land supply situation should be promptly reported to the Shandong Provincial Department of Land and Resources for record by the Qingdao Municipal Land and Resources Department.

It was further found that on October 31, 2002, the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources issued Lao Guo Tu Jia Zi (2002) No. 55 "Reply on Confirming the Result of the Land Valuation," confirming the land valuation result entrusted by Nantai Company from Qingdao Eastern Real Estate Appraisal and Consulting Co., Ltd.

It was also found that on March 1, 2004, the Legal Affairs Office of the Qingdao Municipal People's Government and the Qingdao Municipal Bureau of Land and Resources and Housing Administration jointly issued Qing Fa Zhi (2004) No. 22 "Report on the Situation of Land Use for the 'Australia Garden' Project in Duanjiabu Village, Laoshan District," which proposed the following handling opinion: Given the current situation, the land in question could no longer be transferred by agreement as agreed in the State-owned Land Use Right Grant Contract signed by the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources and Nantai Company on January 6, 2003. The key to resolving this issue is to lawfully terminate the grant contract. However, because the nature of the contract falls within the scope of civil legal relations, and the parties to the contract are the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources and Nantai Company, not the municipal government, the contract should be terminated by the parties to the contract in accordance with the law. For this reason, it was recommended that the municipal government convene a meeting of the Laoshan District Government and relevant units to study and clarify the following matters before having the relevant responsible units organize the implementation according to law: (1) The Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources lawfully terminates the State-owned Land Use Right Grant Contract signed with Nantai Company and refunds the land transfer fee and related expenses. (2) The Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources lawfully perfects the land requisition procedures for the parcel and places it into the government reserve according to law. On March 8, 2004, the General Office of the Qingdao Municipal People's Government, Shandong Province, submitted to the Supervision Office of the Shandong Provincial People's Government "Report on the Situation of Land Use for the 'Australia Garden' Project in Duanjiabu Village, Laoshan District, Qingdao," which proposed the following handling opinion: Given the current situation, the land in question could no longer be transferred by agreement as agreed in the State-owned Land Use Right Grant Contract signed by the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources and Nantai Company on January 6, 2003. The grant contract should be lawfully terminated, the land transfer fee and related expenses refunded, and the parcel placed into the government reserve according to law.

On July 4, 2005, the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources submitted to this Court "Several Supplementary Explanations on the Appeal of the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources v. Qingdao Nantai Real Estate Co., Ltd." In that document, it mentioned that if this Court did not uphold its appeal request, the result would be that the contract could not be performed and the rights claimed by the party could not be realized. It requested this Court to find the facts, render a judgment based on the facts, and even if the contract were found valid, to take into account the factual obstacles—legal and factual—that would prevent the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources from continuing to perform the grant contract in this case, and render a lawful, reasonable, and fair judgment.

On September 1, 2005, the Laoshan District People's Government of Qingdao, Shandong Province submitted to this Court Lao Zheng Han (2005) No. 21 "Letter on the Explanation of the Situation Regarding the Dispute over the State-owned Land Use Right Grant Contract between the District Bureau of Land and Resources and Qingdao Nantai Real Estate Co., Ltd." In that letter, it was mentioned that because the case involved the implementation of provisions by the ministries and commissions of the State Council and the implementation of instructions from State Council leaders, the following explanation was given: (1) In accordance with relevant provisions and the spirit of leaders' instructions, the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources issued on April 14, 2004 the "Notice on Terminating the State-owned Land Use Right Grant Contract"; (2) In accordance with current state-owned land transfer management regulations and the actual situation in Laoshan District, the land grant contract could no longer be performed. For the reasons and specific opinions, please refer to the "Report on the Situation of Land Use for the 'Australia Garden' Project in Duanjiabu Village, Laoshan District" jointly issued by the Legal Affairs Office of the Qingdao Municipal People's Government and the Qingdao Municipal Bureau of Land and Resources and Housing Administration (Qing Fa Zhi (2004) No. 22).

During the second instance of this Court, on March 10, 2005, the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources provided the Criminal Judgment No. (2004) Tai Xing Er Chu Zi No. 20 rendered by the Tai'an Intermediate People's Court of Shandong Province on January 13, 2005. The defendant Yu Zhijun did not appeal within the statutory period, and the judgment has become legally effective. Nantai Company does not object to this. The judgment found: In August 2001, the defendant Yu Zhijun, taking advantage of his position as director of the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources, accepted the request of Lu Guoqiang, the general manager of Qingdao Xincheng Real Estate Co., Ltd., and handled the state-owned land use right reservation procedures for that company. To express gratitude and to continue receiving Yu Zhijun's care, on the day before the Spring Festival in 2002, Lu Guoqiang gave Yu Zhijun a shopping card worth RMB 30,000 from Qingdao Jusco. In January 2003, Yu Zhijun, under the pretext of purchasing a car, demanded RMB 330,000 from Lu Guoqiang. The above acts of Yu Zhijun constituted the crime of accepting bribes, and there was an element of extorting a bribe.

Other facts found by this Court in the second instance are the same as those found by the first-instance court.

This Court holds that there are three focal issues in dispute between the parties in the second instance: first, whether the State-owned Land Use Right Grant Contract signed by the parties has taken effect; second, whether the said contract is valid; and third, whether the first-instance judgment violated the civil litigation principle of "no trial without complaint."

1. Regarding whether the State-owned Land Use Right Grant Contract signed by the parties has taken effect.
Pursuant to Article 45 of the Contract Law of the PRC, the parties may agree on conditions for the effectiveness of a contract. A contract subject to conditions takes effect when the conditions are fulfilled. A contract subject to conditions refers to a contract where the parties specifically agree on certain conditions, and the effectiveness of the contract depends on whether those conditions are fulfilled. The conditions attached to a contract must be future, uncertain events that are agreed upon by the parties, not prescribed by law, and must also be lawful. In China, the authority and duty of government agencies to examine or approve certain matters or contracts derive from the provisions of laws and administrative regulations, and do not fall within the scope of the parties' agreement. If the parties agree that the examining or approving authority of a government agency over certain matters or contracts, as provided by laws and administrative regulations, constitutes a condition in a conditional contract, this is inconsistent with the provisions of the Contract Law on conditional contracts. Similarly, if the parties agree that the examining or approving authority of a government agency over certain matters or contracts, which is not provided for by laws or administrative regulations, constitutes a condition in a conditional contract, this is also inconsistent with the provisions of the Contract Law on conditional contracts. According to the spirit of the Contract Law, if the parties, when concluding a contract, treat a statutory examining or approving authority as a condition for the contract to take effect, it is deemed that no condition has been attached. If a party treats an examining or approving authority that is not provided by law as within the scope of a government agency's duties as a condition for the effectiveness of a civil juristic act, including a contract, it is also deemed that no condition has been attached, and the attached "condition" does not produce the legal effect of limiting the validity of the contract.

Based on the facts found by the first-instance court and this Court, the "Australia Garden" project involved in this case was introduced by the Qingdao Municipal People's Government of Shandong Province during investment attraction activities. The procedures for establishing the project, planning, land use, etc., were approved successively by the relevant functional departments of the Qingdao Municipal People's Government and the relevant functional departments of the Laoshan District People's Government. On December 26, 2002, the Qingdao Municipal People's Government submitted to the Shandong Provincial People's Government the "Request for Instructions on the Eighteenth Batch of Urban Construction Land in 2002 in Laoshan District," which included the land involved in this case. On February 19, 2003, the Shandong Provincial People's Government issued Lu Zheng Tu Zi (2003) No. 52 "Reply on the Approval of the Eighteenth Batch of Urban Construction Land in the Year 2002 in Laoshan District, Qingdao," approving the conversion of 200,000 square meters of agricultural land in Shazikou Subdistrict Office, Laoshan District into construction land. The said agricultural land was approved for requisition after conversion, to be used for urban construction in Qingdao. The reply also indicated that land should be provided to specific construction projects strictly in accordance with relevant provisions, and that the land supply situation should be promptly reported by the Qingdao Municipal Land and Resources Department to the Shandong Provincial Department of Land and Resources for record. This shows that the Shandong Provincial People's Government adopted a record-filing system rather than an approval system for the management of land supply for construction projects, and matters related to land supply did not require approval from the Shandong Provincial People's Government.

In the State-owned Land Use Right Grant Contract, the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources and Nantai Company agreed that "the transfer plan for the parcel under this contract is subject to approval by the Shandong Provincial People's Government, and this contract shall take effect upon the date of approval by the Shandong Provincial People's Government." Although this indicated that the parties agreed that approval by the Shandong Provincial People's Government of the transfer plan for the parcel under the contract would be a condition precedent for the contract to take effect, this condition does not fall within the type of condition precedent for a contract to take effect as provided in the Contract Law. Moreover, the Shandong Provincial People's Government, in its relevant reply, explicitly stated that the situation of land provision for specific construction projects should be promptly reported by the Qingdao Municipal Land and Resources Department to the Shandong Provincial Department of Land and Resources for record, indicating that approval was not required. Therefore, the parties' agreement that the transfer plan for the parcel under the contract required approval by the Shandong Provincial People's Government to take effect does not produce the legal effect of limiting the validity of the State-owned Land Use Right Grant Contract involved in this case. The argument of the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources that the condition precedent for the contract's effectiveness agreed in the State-owned Land Use Right Grant Contract had not been fulfilled, and thus the contract had not taken effect, lacks legal basis. The first-instance court was correct in its application of law when it held that whether the request submitted by the Qingdao Municipal People's Government included the "transfer plan" as agreed in the contract did not affect the validity of the contract.

2. Regarding whether the State-owned Land Use Right Grant Contract signed by the parties is valid.
The State-owned Land Use Right Grant Contract in this case was an agreement reached on the basis of equality and voluntariness, with genuine expression of intent. Pursuant to Article 44 of the Land Administration Law of the PRC, which came into effect on January 1, 1999, where construction occupies land, if the conversion of agricultural land into construction land is involved, the procedures for approval of the conversion of agricultural land must be completed. Within the scale of construction land in cities, villages, and market towns determined by the overall land use plan, for the purpose of implementing that plan, the conversion of agricultural land into construction land shall be approved in batches on a yearly basis by the agency that originally approved the overall land use plan. Within the scope of approved agricultural land conversion, land for specific construction projects may be approved by the people's government of the city or county. The land in dispute in this case has been approved by the Shandong Provincial People's Government under Lu Zheng Tu Zi (2003) No. 52, and is already approved construction land. The land transfer plan should be approved by the people's government of the city or county. Pursuant to Article 22 of the Regulations on the Implementation of the Land Administration Law of the PRC, which came into effect on January 1, 1999, for specific construction projects occupying state-owned construction land within the scale of urban construction land determined by the overall land use plan, the land administrative department of the city or county shall issue a preliminary examination report on the project's land use, the people's government of the city or county shall approve the land supply plan proposed by the land administrative department, and after such approval, the people's government of the city or county shall issue a construction land permit to the construction unit. Thereafter, the land administrative department of the city or county shall sign a state-owned land use right paid-use contract with the land user. In this case, before the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources, as the land administrative department of the city and county level, signed the State-owned Land Use Right Grant Contract with Nantai Company as the land user, although no construction land permit had been issued, this constituted a simplification or omission in the procedures for handling the relevant land supply procedures by the Laoshan District Bureau of Land and Resources, and does not constitute a circumstance that would render the contract invalid under Article 52 of the Contract Law of the PRC.

Shortly after the Laoshan District Land and Resources Bureau and Nantai Company signed the "State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract" on January 6, 2003, the People's Government of Shandong Province approved the procedures for converting agricultural land to construction land and the land acquisition procedures for the parcel under the contract on February 19, 2003, and also required that land be provided to specific construction projects in accordance with relevant regulations and that the land supply situation be reported to the Department of Land and Resources of Shandong Province for record. This indicates that the land under the "State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract" signed by the two parties had undergone the procedures for converting agricultural land to construction land and land acquisition, meeting the conditions stipulated in the "Land Administration Law of the PRC" for the people's government of a city or county to approve land for specific construction projects, and no longer required the land grant plan for the parcel under the contract to be submitted to the People's Government of Shandong Province for approval. The land under the contract met the conditions for construction land and could enter the land grant market. The validity of the "State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract" signed by the two parties on January 6, 2003, was thereby cured, consistent with the spirit of Article 51 of the "Contract Law of the PRC" regarding the validity of a contract where a person without the right of disposition disposes of another's property but later acquires the right of disposition. Therefore, the argument of the Laoshan District Land and Resources Bureau that the "State-owned Land Use Rights Grant Contract" signed by the two parties violated mandatory provisions of laws and administrative regulations and should be deemed invalid has no legal basis and is not supported.

The "Measures of Shandong Province for Implementing the Land Administration Law of the PRC," formulated by the Standing Committee of the Shandong Provincial People's Congress, is a local regulation; the "Regulations on the Grant of State-owned Land Use Rights by Tender, Auction, and Listing," which came into effect on July 1, 2002, is a departmental rule formulated by the Ministry of Land and Resources to strengthen land administration. According to the provisions of Article 52, Item (5) of the "Contract Law of the PRC" and Article 4 of the Supreme People's Court's "Interpretation (I) on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Contract Law of the PRC," which states that "after the implementation of the Contract Law, a people's court confirming a contract as invalid shall be based on laws enacted by the National People's Congress and its Standing Committee and administrative regulations formulated by the State Council, and shall not be based on local regulations or administrative rules," only contracts that violate mandatory provisions of laws and administrative regulations can be confirmed as invalid. Local regulations and administrative rules cannot serve as the basis for confirming a contract as invalid. Therefore, the request of the Laoshan District Land and Resources Bureau to invalidate the contract based on alleged violations of local regulations formulated by the Standing Committee of the Shandong Provincial People's Congress and departmental rules formulated by the Ministry of Land and Resources has no legal basis and is not supported. Furthermore, according to relevant state regulations, if operational land was to be granted by agreement after July 1, 2002, without prior approval from the city or county government or a signed written project development agreement before that date, the grant should be changed to tender, auction, or listing methods in accordance with relevant regulations.
